vignette:
Koa, a sixty-three-year-old publisher, had always thrived on the vibrant energy of his industry. That changed irrevocably three years ago at the National Book Awards gala. He remembered the grand ballroom, the clinking of glasses, and then the deafening roar of an explosion that tore through the historic hotel. Koa was thrown, pinned beneath a fallen beam, and forced to witness the ensuing chaos: the screams, the dust, the injured, and the dead. The overwhelming smell of scorched materials mingled with the sweet, acrid tang of spilled champagne and liquor from overturned tables, a sensory assault that branded itself onto his memory.

In the aftermath, Koa found that his memories of the frightening event were not fading; instead, they remained intensely vivid and visual, forcing their way into his mind at unwanted moments. He would see the faces, the debris, the terror, as clear as if it were yesterday. This vivid, immediate recall meant that even subtle sensory cues or fleeting associations, which might otherwise be dismissed, now possessed an unnerving ability to instantly transport him back to the scene, making them potent and inescapable triggers. These intrusive recollections became so distressing that he began to actively avoid anything that might bring them to the surface. He started to avoid seeing friends, fearing that any casual conversation might veer into difficult topics or that he might be asked to talk about the event, which he knew would trigger an overwhelming flood of those persistent, unwelcome images.

His attempts to control these memories through avoidance, however, inadvertently made certain triggers far more potent. He rarely encountered the specific mix of dust and alcohol from that day, but when he did, such as catching a whiff of cheap liquor at the supermarket, it would hit him with the force of a physical blow, instantly transporting him back to the chaos of the ballroom. Similarly, waking up from a nightmare, the dream residue would linger, a chilling echo of the terror he had experienced, instantly plunging him into a state of profound distress. This constant battle with his mind left him feeling perpetually on edge, even inside his own home. He was certain that danger lurked everywhere, making him feel on guard at all times.

This pervasive sense of threat compelled Koa to adopt a series of defensive behaviours. When he went to his small local cafe or even sat in his own living room, he would always position himself with his back against a wall, needing to see the entire room, convinced that this posture offered some measure of control and safety. He found himself constantly checking his surroundings, scanning for any sign of potential danger, a habit that had become second nature. These very strategies, meant to protect him, paradoxically maintained his heightened state of alert. By always looking for threats, he remained in a hyper-vigilant mode, making him jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not have bothered him before, reinforcing his deeply held belief that the world remained an unpredictable and dangerous place.

What was most insidious was how this heightened state of alert and constant readiness for danger seemed to prime his mind for the traumatic memories. When he was feeling particularly jumpy or easily startled, the vivid, visual recollections of the disaster would force their way into his mind with even greater intensity, making it harder to push them away. And ironically, his attempts to suppress these memories or avoid situations that might trigger them, like his increasing isolation from friends and professional gatherings, seemed only to strengthen their grip. The more he tried not to think about it, the more those vivid pictures of the collapse and the aftermath would intrude, especially during quiet moments when his guard was down.

His once-thriving career as a publisher had suffered immensely. Networking events and book launches, once highlights of his professional life, became unbearable due to his need to sit defensively and his fear of social interaction. His wife, concerned by his increasing withdrawal and constant anxiety, finally urged him to seek help. Koa now felt utterly exhausted, trapped in a relentless cycle where his efforts to feel safe only seemed to perpetuate his fear and the haunting presence of the past. He sought help, desperate to find a way out of the tightening loop that had consumed his life, afraid he would never again know peace.
